cards.explanation: The answer is that God's promise has given him life. The psalmist says, "This is my comfort in affliction, that Your promise has given me life." Notice he doesn't say the trouble got fixed first. I think a comfort that doesn't wait for the trouble to leave is the kind you can carry around in your apron pocket, friends.

The answer is False. The psalmist says, "The arrogant utterly deride me, but I do not turn from Your law." That "but" is doing a lot of heavy lifting, friends. The mocking comes in, and the law stays put.

The answer is the LORD's judgments of old. He says, "I remember Your judgments of old, O LORD, and in them I find comfort." He remembers those judgments and finds comfort in them. Some people scroll for comfort, friends, and he remembers.

The answer is "reject." He says, "Rage has taken hold of me because of the wicked who reject Your law." It's strong language, and the text doesn't soften it. What sets him off is people turning their backs on God's law.

The answer is "songs." The psalmist says, "Your statutes are songs to me in the house of my pilgrimage." God's statutes are songs to him, right there in the house of his pilgrimage. I hum while I stamp, friends, and my mustache sways along.
The answer is True. He says, "In the night, O LORD, I remember Your name, that I may keep Your law." Most of us remember an embarrassing thing from 2009 at 3 a.m. He remembers the LORD's name.

The answer is that he obeys God's precepts. "This is my practice, for I obey Your precepts." The reason he gives is that he obeys, with no long speech attached. Me, friends, I need three paragraphs to explain why I'm late to my own bakery.

The answer is to keep God's words. The verse says, "The LORD is my portion; I have promised to keep Your words." Those two things sit side by side in the same verse, friends. He calls the LORD his portion, and he says he has promised to keep God's words.

The answer is False. He tells God he has sought His face with all his heart, no half measures. "I have sought Your face with all my heart; be gracious to me according to Your promise." That's someone who gave it his all, friends.

The answer is God's testimonies. "I considered my ways and turned my steps to Your testimonies." He considers his ways, and then he turns his steps to God's testimonies. I like that the considering comes first, friends.
The answer is False. The psalmist says, "I hurried without hesitating to keep Your commandments." He hurried, and the verse adds that he didn't hesitate, friends. Taking his time is not what he says.

The answer is to give God thanks. "At midnight I rise to give You thanks for Your righteous judgments." He rises at midnight, and thanks is what he rises for. The thanks is for God's righteous judgments. That's one thankful man, friends.

The answer is "friend." He says, "I am a friend to all who fear You, and to those who keep Your precepts." He is a friend to the people who fear God and keep His precepts. I think a table with friends like that has room for one more chair, friends.

The answer is True. He says, "The earth is filled with Your loving devotion, O LORD; teach me Your statutes." The whole earth is full of it, friends. And right after saying so, he asks God to teach him His statutes.

The answer is True. "Teach me good judgment and knowledge, for I believe in Your commandments." He asks to be taught, and he gives the reason that he believes in God's commandments. The request and the reason come together in one verse, friends. Asking to learn is a good habit at any age.

The answer is that he went astray. The psalmist is honest about it: "Before I was afflicted, I went astray…" Nobody likes admitting that, friends. I once tried to stamp a cookie upside down, so I know the feeling.
The answer is False. Before he was afflicted he went astray, "but now I keep Your word." Now he keeps it, friends. He doesn't say he struggles.

The answer is "delights." The psalmist says, "Their hearts are callous and insensitive, but I delight in Your law." Callous hearts on one side, and delight on the other. Delight is the word he picks for his own heart, friends.

The answer is so he might learn God's statutes. "It was good for me to be afflicted, that I might learn Your statutes." He doesn't say the affliction itself was fun, friends. He says it was good for him, and the reason he gives is that he might learn God's statutes.

The answer is thousands of pieces of gold and silver. He says, "The law from Your mouth is more precious to me than thousands of pieces of gold and silver." That's the comparison he makes, friends. He calls the law more precious to him than all of that.
